newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy Ross sees Hebron agreement soon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy Ross sees Hebron agreement soon.

text.p: U.S. mediator Dennis Ross said on Wednesday differences between Israel and the Palestinians over the West Bank town of Hebron were "clearly bridgeable" and he expected an agreement soon.

Contrary to gloomy assessments in the Middle East, Ross, who left the Israeli-Palestinian talks on Monday and returned to Washington, said the three weeks of negotiations he chaired had made considerable progress.

"The differences that remain at this point are clearly bridgeable, they can be overcome, and I believe in fact that reaching an agreement soon is very definitely something that could be done," Ross told a news conference.
The two sides have been struggling to hammer out terms for a partial Israeli withdrawal from Hebron where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Arabs.
Israel has already redeployed in six other West Bank towns, making way for Palestinian self-rule there and in Gaza under peace agreements between the two sides.

Ross returned to Washington after Palestinian President Yasser Arafat left the Middle East for a European tour. Ross denied a statement on Monday by the Israeli ambassador to Washington, Eliahu Ben Elissar, that he had asked Arafat to call off the trip, saying he did "not express a preference that he stay."
Israeli officials have accused Arafat of stalling on the talks, while the Palestinians have blamed Israel for the failure to reach agreement so far.
Lower-level negotiations are continuing in the absence of Arafat and Ross.
Ross said there was "basic agreement" on a transfer of civil authority in Hebron and "substantial agreement" on military aspects of an Israeli pullback, although some issues remained unresolved.

He did not identify the issues, but Israeli and Palestinian officials say they concern Israeli rights of "hot pursuit" into PLO-controlled areas after any guerrilla attack and the type of arms to be used by Palestinian police.

Ross said he could return to the region but "wouldn't plan to go out again until we're at a point where I've had a chance to talk with both parties and we've made a judgment as to whether or not it's appropriate to raise the level."
He said he would be unable to go before next Tuesday's U.S. presidential election, because his youngest daughter was scheduled to have minor surgery on Monday.
The State Department meanwhile denounced what it called the "senseless killing" of an 11-year-old Palestinian boy, allegedly by a Jewish settler in the West Bank.

Hilmi Shousha died of a brain haemorrhage on Monday. Palestinians said the security chief of a Jewish settlement next to his village hit him on the head with a pistol butt, but Israeli settlers said the man had not beaten him.
"We think that this was a senseless tragedy, a senseless killing, and we encourage the Israeli authorities to investigate it completely," Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
In an unusual move apparently designed to draw attention to the incident, the U.S. Consul-General in Jerusalem, Edward Abington, paid a condolence call on Wednesday on the Shousha family.
"By going there, obviously we're expressing our very deep concerns about the fact that an 11-year-old boy was murdered," Burns said. "It's the kind of thing we want to stop."
